Debug and trace logging did not expose the token endpoint HTTP status or response body.

items.title: Fix daemon updater socket binding and bootstrap readiness on Unix
items.body:
Fix daemon updater socket binding and bootstrap readiness on Unix

## Why

The updater bound its socket directly beneath `CODEX_HOME`, which can exceed Unix socket path limits. Bootstrap could also report success before the updater's manual-update socket was ready.

## What changed

- Reuse the control socket's protected binding and cleanup guard for the updater, with a symlink at the advertised socket path.
- Remove stale updater socket entries before startup while preserving regular files.
- Wait up to 30 seconds for supported automatic updaters to publish their socket, without connecting as a readiness probe. Report updater exit or timeout with stderr log context.
- Preserve compatibility with older updaters that lack the manual-update command.

## Testing

Add Unix integration tests for updater readiness with a long `CODEX_HOME` path and bootstrap failure when a regular file blocks the updater socket, verifying that the file is preserved and the daemon remains running.

items.title: [macOS Desktop] codex reaches 73.9 GB footprint during memory_stage1 extraction of a 26.3 GB history

items.body:
## Summary
The bundled codex backend repeatedly reaches tens of gigabytes during ordinary ChatGPT desktop use on a 24 GB Mac. New read-only diagnostics identify a running memory_stage1 job for a 26,315,095,941-byte saved history, repeated loads of that same history before three incidents, and stable sampled worker stacks in memory-history serialization and secret redaction. The latest process sample reports a 73.9G physical footprint; its allocation summary is dominated by native malloc regions, much of which is swapped out.

A macOS application-memory warning was followed shortly by a Codex crash. I manually restarted the Mac afterward. The reboot was a recovery action; no automatic reboot, kernel panic, or verified application-crash cause is claimed.

This appears closely related to #53039 and #51233. Please consolidate if appropriate. This adds macOS evidence on the same bundled backend version as #53039, two matching stack captures, a 26.3 GB history, and detailed heap/swap measurements.

The 26.3 GB chat history loaded and functioned normally in the foreground for days without issue; the runaway memory growth only occurs when the background memory_stage1 extraction job attempts to process it.

## Environment
- ChatGPT desktop: 26.1007.30912, build 20156 (installed bundle metadata).
- Bundled backend: codex-cli 0.162.0-alpha.17.2 (bundled executable --version).
- Codex Framework: 155.0.8059.40 (running executable paths).
- macOS: 27.0.1, build 26A434; ARM64.
- Hardware identifier: Mac18,5; 24 GB RAM.
- Startup filesystem had approximately 121.5 GiB available during capture.
- Existing profile; no clean-install reproduction performed.
- Relevant configuration, read without changes:
  [features]
  memories = true
  [memories]
  generate_memories = true
  use_memories = true

## Measured timeline
All times below are October 13, 2026, America/Chicago (UTC-05:00).

1. 16:39:37: backend diagnostic log records loading the large history (History A, 26,315,095,941 bytes) alongside another history. A prior support investigation reported a 55.0G footprint for this earlier launch; that prior sample was not remeasured here. This load is now independently verified from the backend log.
2. 19:39:27: the same History A is loaded again. A second history loaded simultaneously reports context_length_exceeded six seconds later. That error belongs to the smaller history and must not be misattributed to History A.
3. 19:47:55: an Activity Monitor sample confirms footprint/peak 71.5G. Its sampled worker remains in serialize_filtered_rollout_response_items -> redact_secrets -> regex search for 2,149 observations. The process Memory column showed 71.47 GB; system swap 65.92 GB; compressed memory 11.79 GB; yellow memory pressure. The visible renderer and ChatGPT parent were approximately 762 MB and 359 MB.
4. A macOS memory warning was followed shortly by a Codex crash, I then manually restarted the Mac. No matching panic or Codex/ChatGPT application crash report was found by a date/name check in the two standard diagnostic-report directories inspected.
5. 19:57:54: the currently sampled backend launches after the reboot.
6. 20:42:12: memory job metadata shows kind=memory_stage1, status=running, started_at=20:42:12, lease_until=21:42:12, finished_at=NULL, retry_remaining=3 for History A. Backend logs show the same history loading at the same second. Another 392,866,603-byte history loads concurrently and fails at 20:42:18 with context_length_exceeded.
7. Around 20:45: Activity Monitor shows the new backend at 43.83 GB, system swap 33.27 GB, and compressed memory 12.06 GB. The largest visible renderer is 596 MB, and ChatGPT parent 339 MB.
8. 20:52:37: a three-second process sample (10 ms sampling interval) reports footprint/peak 73.9G. The relevant worker remains in the same memory-serialization/redaction path for all 265 captured observations.
9. 20:52:41: vmmap -summary also reports footprint/peak 73.9G. A later process-list check confirms the same backend PID is still running; no diagnostic command terminated it.

## Allocation evidence
Selected vmmap values, retaining the tool's reported units:
- Writable regions: total 93.2G; resident 2.7G; swapped out 71.3G; unallocated 19.3G.
- Malloc Large: virtual size 62.8G; resident/dirty 1.6G; swapped 58.3G.
- Malloc Small: virtual size 13.1G; resident/dirty 560.3M; swapped 12.3G.
- Mapped files: 35.2M virtual; 464K resident; no swapped bytes reported.
- Stack: 374.4M virtual; 5.6M resident; 13.5M swapped.
- Total process resident size: approximately 3.1G, despite footprint 73.9G.

The malloc zones dominate the observed footprint; it is not simply a 74 GB mapped file or virtual-address reservation. The zone table separately reports 89.3G bytes allocated. This metric differs from footprint; no claim is made that each value represents the same accounting basis. No allocation-origin heap profile was captured.

## Sampled execution lead
Both independently captured high-footprint processes include:
```text
  codex_memories_write::phase1::job::serialize_filtered_rollout_response_items
  codex_secrets::sanitizer::redact_secrets
  regex_automata search
```

Combined with the exact current memory job/history/load-time match, this strongly points to automatic background memory extraction of oversized stored history. It does not identify the exact allocation stack retaining every byte, prove why the history grew so large, or establish whether redaction itself is responsible for the allocations. The largest history was last modified at 06:28 CDT, hours before the current job. Its contents were not read or uploaded in this investigation; only size and associated job metadata were inspected.

## Observed steps and reproduction status
1. Run ChatGPT desktop 26.1007.30912 with the existing profile and the memory-generation settings listed above. The profile contains a 26,315,095,941-byte saved chat history.
2. Use the app normally. The exact foreground chat/navigation and the event that selected this history for processing have not been established.
3. The backend claims a memory_stage1 job for that history and logs loading it. In the latest occurrence, both timestamps are 20:42:12 CDT.
4. During that occurrence, observe codex reach 43.83 GB in Activity Monitor around 20:45, then a 73.9G footprint in sample/vmmap around 20:52. Both high-footprint stack captures show the history-serialization/redaction path.
5. In an earlier occurrence, a macOS memory warning was followed shortly by a Codex crash, prompting a manual restart. After relaunch, the same history was selected again and the growth recurred.

This is an observed sequence, not a claim that the foreground actions alone deterministically reproduce the problem. The private history has not been replayed in a separate test environment.

## Expected and actual behavior
Expected: background extraction applies a byte/record/memory bound before materializing or serializing a very large history; oversized inputs fail safely or are skipped, and one old chat cannot exhaust the machine. A failed or interrupted job should not repeatedly load the same fatal input without effective safeguards.
Actual: the same 26.3 GB saved history is loaded before repeated runaway episodes, with a currently running extraction job, 71.5G and 73.9G sampled footprints, severe system swap, and a reported memory-warning crash.

## Reproduction status and limitations
- This is an observed existing-profile failure, not a credential-free controlled reproduction.
- No additional large-history load was deliberately triggered. Cloning/replaying the 26.3 GB input would add unnecessary pressure to this already affected machine.
- No configuration, database, history, or application files were changed during diagnosis; local report/evidence files were created. No process was killed.
- A bounded desktop-log inspection also finds background access-denied history reads and ResizeObserver errors. These are secondary observations and do not establish the cause of native backend allocation. The memory-job and stack evidence is stronger.
- Disk activity and swap counts do not quantify NAND wear. A prior macOS codex disk-writes resource diagnostic records approximately 8.59 GB file-backed memory dirtied over roughly 10 hours on October 12; that is neither a swap-write count nor an SSD-health assessment.

## Related reports
- #53039: background extraction of inactive oversized history on Linux, backend 0.162.0-alpha.17.2. Closest version/path comparison; the other report's private input and allocation profile differ.
- #51233: automatic extraction of image-heavy histories and repeated OOM on backend 0.160.0. Similar pipeline and retry concern; this history's image/content composition has not been established.
- #36971: other macOS native heap growth. Older version and different sampled symbols.

## Summary

When the TUI resumes a session whose latest turn is still in progress, the status indicator appears to restart its elapsed timer instead of reflecting the turn's original start time. The status can therefore show approximately `0s` even when the turn has been running much longer.

## Source trace

The replay path receives `started_at` for each turn, but the `TurnStatus::InProgress` branch calls `on_task_started()` without passing or restoring that timestamp. `on_task_started()` resets the status timer to zero. The live start notification and replay path therefore use different timing information.

## Expected behavior

For a replayed in-progress turn with a start timestamp, initialize the status timer from that timestamp so the elapsed indicator continues across reconnect/resume. Keep the zero-time behavior for a genuinely new live turn.

## Reproduction

1. Start a turn and leave it running long enough for the status indicator to show elapsed time.
2. Reopen or resume that thread in the TUI while the turn remains active.
3. Observe that the status timer starts near zero rather than showing the elapsed duration.

This is a TUI replay/status issue, separate from thread ownership or active-writer locking.

### What issue are you seeing?

When using Codex Desktop's **Selected text** feature, the exact selected string can apparently be overridden or substituted by a semantically similar/high-salience entity from earlier conversation context.

This has happened multiple times recently with similar names/entities.

A concrete example from one conversation:

```text
# Selected text:

## Selection 1
command code
```

The follow-up question was about that selected text, but the assistant answered about **OpenCode Go** instead and continued reasoning as if `OpenCode Go` were the intended entity.

The important part is that the UI showed the exact selected string `command code`, yet the resulting answer behaved as though a different, semantically related term from prior conversation history had higher priority.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

The issue is intermittent, but this is the observed pattern:

1. Use a long-running Codex Desktop conversation containing several recurring named entities with similar wording.
2. Select an exact term from a previous message using **Selected text / Add to chat**.
3. Confirm that the composer visibly contains the exact selected string.
4. Ask a short follow-up about that selection.
5. In some cases, the assistant answers about a different but semantically similar entity that was prominent in earlier conversation context.

Observed example:

- Exact selected text: `command code`
- Entity the assistant answered about: `OpenCode Go`

### What is the expected behavior?

Explicit current-turn **Selected text** should have stronger precedence than fuzzy/semantic matches from prior conversation history or retrieved context.

If the selected string is `command code`, the model should receive and reason about that exact string. It should not silently normalize or substitute it with another entity merely because that other entity is semantically similar or frequently mentioned earlier in the conversation.

If the model is uncertain whether two similarly named entities are the same, it should preserve the exact selected string or ask for clarification rather than silently replacing it.

### What is the actual behavior?

A semantically similar/high-frequency entity from prior conversation context can appear to override the explicit selected text, causing the assistant to answer the wrong question even though the UI visibly shows the correct selection.

### Why this matters

Selected text is specifically used to disambiguate references in long conversations. If historical semantic context can override the exact selection, the feature becomes unreliable for:

- product/provider names
- commands
- model names
- files/symbols
- similarly named technical entities

This is especially damaging in long-running technical threads where several related products or tools recur frequently.

- #22670 — selected text references are not shown in sent user messages/history

items.title: Track content provenance through prompt assembly and compaction
items.body:
Track content provenance through prompt assembly and compaction

## Why

Message roles and content classifications do not identify who supplied each context part. Source attribution needs to survive prompt assembly and history truncation, including messages that combine text from different producers.

## What changed

- Add per-part `ContentItemMetadata` for user input, developer instructions, `AGENTS.md`, skills, harness context, command hooks, and tool context with optional callable namespaces.
- Carry attribution alongside content and classifications through contextual fragments, extension prompts, hook output, and agent messages. Keep tool-provided context-window hints separate from harness text.
- Preserve the source of retained text slices during compaction and attribute generated truncation notices to the harness. Default missing historical attribution to unknown.
- Attribute host MCP calls using cached tool namespaces only when catalog revisions remain stable, without starting servers or refreshing catalogs for attribution.
- Send the new metadata to Responses Lite and strip it from requests to endpoints that do not support it.

## Testing

Extend compaction tests to cover mixed sources, missing or extra metadata entries, and discarded media. Update Responses Lite request assertions to verify endpoint-specific attribution handling.

items.body:
Prune unused app-server daemon releases safely

## What changed

- Record the current and previous dedicated daemon selections in `selection-history`, bound to the selection link's identity. Preserve that history when an install leaves the selection unchanged.

- Require lifecycle and installer locks, valid selection history, and verified package boundaries before cleanup. Skip unsafe or unrecognized packages and retire releases before best-effort deletion so partial failures are not retried.
- Resolve the updater's actual executable identity after an executable handoff that preserves its PID.

## Testing

Extend coverage for stale selection history, retention of the last two selections, packages containing external symlinks, partial deletion and reinstall, cleanup without restarting the daemon, and repeated installs preserving selection history.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

OpenAI.Codex (Windows MSIX package): 26.1007.2314.0 About ChatGPT (Powered by Codex & OWL): 26.1007.21434 (released October 9, 2026)

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Plus

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 21H2, version 10.0.19044 (build 19044), x64

### What issue are you seeing?


## Summary

Codex Desktop intermittently marks a file-backed Goal as `complete` after reading `goal-objective.md`, without performing the substantive user task stored in that file.

The failure is confirmed by the original Codex session JSONL: the agent called `update_goal(status="complete")`, the tool confirmed the transition, and the agent stopped despite the actual task being unfinished.

A separate successful control session using the same file-backed objective mechanism behaved correctly and continued executing the substantive task for approximately 21 minutes before completing the Goal.

This is an **intermittent premature Goal-completion bug**. The exact root cause has not been established.

## Observed behavior

The original user objective required a multi-stage technical investigation, experiments, validation, and a final report.

Codex represented the persistent Goal using an internal transport instruction:

`Read the Codex goal objective file at [REDACTED]/goal-objective.md before continuing.`

After loading the objective file and performing limited preliminary operations, the agent queried its Goal state and then marked the Goal complete.

Its final response indicated that the **file-reading objective** had been completed. However, the substantive investigation and required deliverables were not finished.

The completion was not merely a misleading text response: the actual Goal-management tool confirmed `status="complete"`.

## Evidence: premature completion

Extracted directly from the failing Codex session JSONL. All timestamps below are UTC.

| Timestamp | JSONL line | Event | Result |
|---|---:|---|---|
| 2026-10-13 23:06:35.530 | 14 | `thread_goal_updated` | `active`, 0 tokens, 0 seconds |
| 2026-10-13 23:06:38.378 | 17 | Objective-file tool call | Initial objective processing |
| 2026-10-13 23:06:49.966 | 32 | Objective-file tool call | Further objective processing |
| 2026-10-13 23:06:53.860 | 36 | `get_goal` call | Goal state queried |
| 2026-10-13 23:06:55.644 | 39 | `get_goal` result | `active`, 19,856 tokens, 14 seconds |
| 2026-10-13 23:06:59.844 | 43 | `update_goal` call | `status="complete"` |
| 2026-10-13 23:06:59.905 | 45 | `update_goal` result | `complete`, 21,399 tokens, 24 seconds |
| 2026-10-13 23:07:05.038 | 51 | `task_complete` | Execution stops |

The `get_goal` and `update_goal` calls were identified from actual tool-call records, and their results were matched using tool-call identifiers.

No completed substantive research deliverables existed at the point of this Goal completion.

## Evidence: successful control

A separate file-backed Goal session did not exhibit premature completion.

| Timestamp | JSONL line | Event | Result |
|---|---:|---|---|
| 2026-10-13 23:29:23.765 | 14 | `thread_goal_updated` | `active`, 0 tokens, 0 seconds |
| 2026-10-13 23:29:26.698 | 17 | Objective-file tool call | Objective processing |
| 2026-10-13 23:29:34.515 | 30 | `task_complete` | Initial turn finishes |
| 2026-10-13 23:29:38.999 | 38 | Other tool call | Substantive execution continues |
| 2026-10-13 23:50:15.614 | 568 | `update_goal` call | `status="complete"` |
| 2026-10-13 23:50:16.557 | 571 | `update_goal` result | `complete`, 186,770 tokens, 1,252 seconds |
| 2026-10-13 23:50:21.965 | 577 | `task_complete` | Final turn finishes |

The successful control contained multiple intermediate turns and 64 non-Goal tool calls classified in the sanitized trace before the final Goal completion.

### Key difference

- **Failing session:** Goal marked complete after 24 seconds of reported Goal usage, before completing the user task.
- **Successful control:** Goal remained in progress for approximately 21 minutes, with substantive tool-driven work before completion.

The token counts and durations above are values reported by the Goal-management tool. They are not independently verified billing figures.

The two sessions establish a behavioral difference, not a confirmed explanation for that difference.

## Impact

A persistent Goal can incorrectly transition to `complete` even though its actual completion criteria remain unsatisfied.

This undermines the reliability of long-running, autonomous workflows because Codex can report success and stop working without producing the requested results.

The observed defect is distinct from an ordinary `task_complete` event that ends an individual turn while the Goal remains active.


### What steps can reproduce the bug?


1. Open Codex Desktop and start a new Goal.
2. Provide a large, substantive objective requiring multiple operations and verifiable deliverables, such as investigating a software problem, running experiments, validating results, and producing a report.
3. Use an objective large enough for Codex to transport it through an internal `goal-objective.md` attachment.
4. Allow the agent to load and read the objective file.
5. Observe Goal-state transitions and whether the agent continues the substantive task.

**Observed intermittent failure:** After loading the objective and carrying out only preliminary steps, the agent calls `update_goal(status="complete")` and reports completion of the file-reading instruction rather than the user's actual objective.

**Reproduction status:** One failure has been confirmed using the original session JSONL, with a separate successful control session. Additional synthetic attempts did not reliably reproduce the failure.

The sanitized evidence contains original JSONL line numbers, timestamps, Goal tool-call/result pairs, and reported usage counters. Raw session identifiers, private objectives, source code, and local filesystem paths are intentionally omitted from public attachments.

A deterministic minimal reproduction and the exact triggering condition are not yet known.


### What is the expected behavior?


A file-backed Goal must preserve the substantive user objective and its completion criteria.

Reading `goal-objective.md` should be treated only as an initialization step, not as successful completion of the Goal.

The agent should continue executing the requested investigation, validation, and deliverables until the actual completion criteria are satisfied or an explicit blocking condition requires user intervention.

`update_goal(status="complete")` should only be used after the substantive objective has been fulfilled.

Intermediate `task_complete` events should remain separate from completion of the persistent Goal.

In particular, successful execution of the internal instruction to read the objective file must never, by itself, satisfy a multi-stage user Goal.



### Additional information

## Possible cause — not confirmed

The agent or Goal-management mechanism may be treating the internal file-loading instruction as the effective Goal completion criterion rather than evaluating the actual substantive objective.

Potential investigation areas include:

- File-backed objective materialization and persistence.
- The distinction between the transport instruction and the substantive Goal.
- The interaction between Goal state, tool results, and completion decisions.
- Validation of `update_goal(status="complete")` against the original objective.

No specific internal root cause has been demonstrated.

## Suggested regression test

Create a large multi-stage Goal transported through `goal-objective.md`, with verifiable required deliverables.

After reading the objective file, verify that the Goal remains active and the agent continues working until those deliverables are complete.

Run the test repeatedly because the observed failure is intermittent.

## Sanitized evidence

Two metadata-only timelines are attached:

- `FAILED-public.txt`: the initial failing sequence, ending at the first premature `task_complete`.
- `SUCCESS-public.txt`: a successful file-backed Goal session through normal completion.

The evidence contains timestamps, event classifications, original JSONL line numbers, Goal statuses, matched call references, and usage counters.

No full conversation messages, original objective text, command bodies, source code, usernames, absolute paths, or attachment UUIDs are included.

## Related issues

- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/42012 — file-backed Goal attachment wrapper handling.
- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/41831 — Goal continuation and lifecycle behavior.
- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/39715 — related premature Goal completion, but involving scope narrowing rather than completion of a file-backed objective-loading step.

These issues may involve related lifecycle mechanisms, but a shared root cause has not been established.

Support daemon installation from Windows WinGet packages

## Why

WinGet archives place the CLI and code mode host at the package root, while daemon installation expects them under `bin/`. This layout mismatch prevents installing the daemon from a WinGet CLI package.

Validate WinGet packages in their original layout before converting the staged copy to the daemon layout. Move the executables under `bin/`, update the package entrypoint and optional voice manifest checksum key, and hash the final tree for release reuse. Leave the source package unchanged.

## Testing

Add a Windows integration test covering daemon startup, repeated `update --from-cli --yes` calls, rewritten manifests, and rejection of an incomplete package without changing the selected release or source manifests.

Other conversations using the same model completed around the initial failure, including successful inputs larger than the affected conversation's last successful input. Those observations prompted a history-specific investigation rather than an assumption of account-wide failure.

## Isolation method and results

I read a backup of the affected history and progressively bisected its 146 saved reasoning items. Direct HTTPS requests went to the built-in OpenAI Responses endpoint, used `store=false`, declared `tools=[]`, and never executed tools or modified the production conversation.

The requests matched the native 0.161.0 Responses Lite settings: `x-openai-internal-codex-responses-lite: true`, `reasoning.context=all_turns`, `parallel_tool_calls=false`, and High effort. A fixed diagnostic prompt-cache key was used. The saved ciphertext was not changed.

| Diagnostic input | Model / service tier | Observed result |
|---|---|---|
| Neutral prompt, no saved reasoning | GPT-6.1 Sol / default | 4/4 completed |
| All 146 saved reasoning items, without original conversation messages, tool results or goal prompts | GPT-6.1 Sol / default | `server_error` |
| One isolated original reasoning item + neutral prompt; 8,894 bytes | GPT-6.1 Sol / default | 4/4 `server_error` |
| Same isolated item; 8,920 bytes | GPT-6.1 Sol / Priority | 2/2 `server_error` |
| Remaining 145 reasoning items after removing only the isolated item; about 939 KB | GPT-6.1 Sol / default | 3/3 completed; 53,165 input tokens each |
| Same remaining 145 items | GPT-6.1 Sol / Priority | 1/1 completed |
| Isolated item with its ID and internal message metadata omitted; ciphertext unchanged | GPT-6.1 Sol / default | 2/2 `server_error` |
| Same original isolated item, including unchanged ciphertext | GPT-6 Sol / default, High | 3/3 completed |
| Adjacent saved reasoning item | GPT-6.1 Sol / default | Completed |

These are bounded diagnostic trials. The exact backend component and exception remain unknown. The evidence isolates an input-dependent upstream processing failure associated with this saved reasoning state; it does not identify a universal size limit or establish that the original ciphertext was locally corrupted.

## Minimal request shape

The private saved item is omitted here. The placeholder is not a standalone runnable fixture, and synthetic ciphertext will not reproduce the same condition.

Relevant non-authentication header:

```text
x-openai-internal-codex-responses-lite: true
```

```json
{
  "model": "gpt-6.1-sol",
  "instructions": "Diagnostic request. Reply exactly OK. Do not use any tools.",
  "input": [
    {
      "type": "reasoning",
      "summary": [],
      "encrypted_content": "<original saved ciphertext retained privately>"
    },
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content": [{"type": "input_text", "text": "Reply exactly OK."}]
    }
  ],
  "tools": [],
  "parallel_tool_calls": false,
  "stream": true,
  "store": false,
  "reasoning": {"effort": "high", "summary": "auto", "context": "all_turns"},
  "include": ["reasoning.encrypted_content"],
  "service_tier": "priority"
}
```

The original item ID and metadata were preserved in the initial experiments. Removing them also failed, as shown above. The default-tier controls omitted `service_tier`. All compared requests used the same neutral instructions and prompt.

The failing SSE contained both an `error` event with `type=server_error, code=server_error` and a `response.failed` event with `error.code=server_error`, before any model output. This distinguishes the observed upstream error from a lost network connection despite the CLI's stream-disconnection wording.

## Request IDs for backend correlation

All times below are UTC. The account owner has authorized publication of these diagnostic request IDs, which are necessary for backend correlation.

| Request | UTC timestamp | Request ID |
|---|---|---|
| Original native-session terminal failure | 2026-10-13 23:53:48 | `63536b58-2297-4c73-8a04-190b25bdad2b` |
| Isolated item, GPT-6.1 Sol Priority, failed | 2026-10-14 00:06:12 | `cb93a09c-ed0d-40cf-8d77-e6d4dd73f27a` |
| Same isolated item, Priority repeat, failed | 2026-10-14 00:06:13 | `389cdfd5-d868-4ec7-b246-5f77e2383f89` |
| Isolated item without ID/metadata, failed | 2026-10-14 00:05:27 | `d23aa8ea-f722-4eb4-8be9-f244f483922b` |
| Same original isolated item, GPT-6 Sol High, completed | 2026-10-14 00:04:50 | `66f516f4-a84e-4744-aee8-d28f831dcc18` |
| Other 145 items, GPT-6.1 Sol Priority, completed | 2026-10-14 00:06:39 | `2a199920-ee26-46fc-a615-f8c85956cc32` |

## Recovery actually performed

Before the single-item diagnosis was complete, I backed up the original history and goal, unloaded the affected conversation, and manually appended a replacement active-context record that omitted the 146 invisible reasoning items and 21 repeated automatic goal-continuation prompts. The original visible history, prior compaction item, tool call/results, conversation identity and goal were retained. Existing transcript bytes were preserved.

After reloading the same conversation, the same GPT-6.1 Sol model resumed the original task and completed 28 tool calls without a new terminal error during the first approximately nine minutes of observation. This is a manually applied workaround, not an official or permanent backend fix. Subsequent direct single-item replay established that a goal-continuation prompt was not needed to trigger the failure.

## Expected behavior and requested investigation

1. A reasoning state returned by the service should remain processable on subsequent supported requests, or fail with an actionable compatibility explanation.
2. Please correlate the failing and successful request IDs to identify the backend component/exception and whether this matches #53143.
3. Please advise on a supported recovery method that preserves a conversation and its goal when a retained reasoning item triggers repeated processing failures.
4. If a saved-state compatibility or worker/deployment change is responsible, please provide a fix or an explicit supported mitigation.

No original prompts, answers, task objective, conversation title, thread IDs, private reasoning ciphertext, raw transcripts, credentials, account identifiers, personal filesystem paths or private service addresses are included. The private minimal fixture is retained locally; it has not been uploaded publicly. If needed, please identify an official private channel and the minimum diagnostic material required.

items.title: Nested Linux Codex sandbox fails before command execution: masked daemon directory (000) conflicts with inner 0700 check

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

items.body:
## Summary

On Codex CLI **0.162.1** (standalone Linux `aarch64-unknown-linux-musl`), a Codex sandbox invoked from inside another standard Codex sandbox fails **before executing even `/bin/true`**.

The outer sandbox intentionally hides the shared app-server rendezvous directory `/tmp/codex-daemon-<uid>` under a read-only tmpfs with mode `000`. The inner Codex sandbox then calls `prepare_shared_daemon_socket_directory()` on the same fixed path, requires mode `0700`, and refuses to initialize. No model, network access, API credentials, or project files are involved.

## Minimal reproduction

Run as a normal Linux user with the Codex CLI on `PATH`. Pin the same installed binary for the inner invocation:

```bash
CODEX_BIN="$(readlink -f "$(command -v codex)")"
codex --version

# Direct command: PASS (exit 0)
"$CODEX_BIN" sandbox --permission-profile :read-only -- /bin/true

# Nested command: FAIL (exit 1), before /bin/true executes
"$CODEX_BIN" sandbox --permission-profile :workspace -- \
  "$CODEX_BIN" sandbox --permission-profile :read-only -- /bin/true
```

Reproduced in an ordinary user session on Linux ARM64. The failure also reproduces under the outer workspace sandbox variant with the following flags, but these are **not required** for the minimal reproduction:

```text
-c sandbox_workspace_write.network_access=true
-c sandbox_workspace_write.exclude_slash_tmp=true
-c sandbox_workspace_write.exclude_tmpdir_env_var=true
```

## Actual behavior

The direct `/bin/true` invocation exits 0. The nested invocation exits 1:

```text
error building bubblewrap command: app-server socket directory must be a user-owned directory with mode 0700
```

Measured using the same UID/EUID/GID/EGID (1000) in both invocations:

| Object | Direct host view | Outer Codex sandbox view |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/tmp/codex-daemon-1000` | UID 1000, mode `0700` | UID 1000, mode `000` |
| Directory mount | Normal host directory | Read-only tmpfs overlay with `mode=000,uid=1000,gid=1000` |
| `codex-linux-sandbox` executable | Present/executable | Present/executable |

The expected `~/.codex/app-server-control` directory was independently checked as mode `0700`; it is **not** the failing path. Changing `CODEX_HOME` to the default did not resolve it. `HOME`, `TMPDIR`, and `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` do not change the fixed daemon-directory selection.

## Evidence from v0.162.1 source

- [`codex-rs/uds/src/daemon_directory.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.1/codex-rs/uds/src/daemon_directory.rs): `shared_daemon_socket_directory()` derives `canonicalize("/tmp")/codex-daemon-<euid>`; `prepare_shared_daemon_socket_directory()` checks ownership and exact `0700` mode.
- [`codex-rs/linux-sandbox/src/bwrap.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.1/codex-rs/linux-sandbox/src/bwrap.rs): the outer sandbox mounts a mode-`000` mask over that same daemon location.

This creates a conflict between the **security boundary of the outer sandbox** and the **precondition enforced by the inner sandbox**. The host directory itself has correct ownership and permissions. A regular sandbox command works; only nested initialization fails.

## Expected behavior

A second Codex process should be able to run under the same restrictive Linux sandbox guarantees, or report nested sandbox execution as explicitly unsupported with a clear explanation. A supported design should preserve the masking of privileged app-server sockets rather than make them accessible to the nested process.

Please consider handling an already-masked daemon root during nested sandbox setup without reducing IPC isolation, and add a regression test for direct vs nested `/bin/true`.

## Impact

This prevents an outer Codex agent from invoking a second Codex CLI worker with its own normal read-only sandbox. A separately launched Codex CLI worker works on the same host. This is independent of which model/provider the inner Codex uses.

No host chmod/chown change, sandbox bypass, privileged workaround, custom IPC bridge, or binary patch was used.

## Related

- #51520 has a similar error string on another environment, but does **not** demonstrate this specific nested mode-`000` masking conflict; this is a separate, minimal reproducible case.

## Observed failure

Codex CLI `0.162.0-alpha.17.2` on Windows 11 26H2 build `26300.9711` fails before launching a synthetic-only payload when the explicit elevated sandbox applies deny-read rules to an OS-managed directory.

The recorded diagnostic chain is:

```text
windows sandbox failed: helper_unknown_error: apply deny-read ACLs
apply deny-read ACE to C:\ProgramData
open deny ACL target for update
Access is denied. (os error 5)
```

The helper had already added two deny ACEs to an owned protected directory before this failure. The exact captured pre-test DACL of that directory was restored and verified afterward. No payload or native canary test executed. No credential contents were read.

This reports one observed invocation and its side effect, not a claim that every elevated configuration fails.

## Selected implementation and policy

The vendor elevated setup had provisioned dedicated lower-privilege sandbox users and firewall rules. MXC had separately reported unavailable. The failed invocation explicitly selected `windows.sandbox=elevated`, `features.prefer_mxc=false`, a named permission profile and `--include-managed-config`.

The following is the redacted policy structure of the existing failed invocation, not a newly executed minimal reproduction:

```text
:root = read
<founder-profile> = deny
<owned-production-tree> = deny
C:/ProgramData = deny
C:/Windows/ServiceProfiles = deny
<synthetic-workspace> = write
<synthetic-workspace>/forbidden = deny
<synthetic-workspace>/readonly = read
network.enabled = false
```

The payload was a synthetic-only PowerShell script. It never started. An earlier invocation containing an additional deny for `C:/Windows/System32/config` failed during canonicalization; the current invocation omitted only that additional rule. No other deny was removed.

## Privilege evidence and limits

The launcher/controller was a standard non-admin process. Vendor provisioning and read-only security-descriptor collection used separately approved administrator helpers. No administrator payload or founder-credential fallback was permitted.

The diagnostic identifies `codex-windows-sandbox-setup.exe` as the ACL-applying helper. Its exact runtime or impersonation token and the failed CLI token were not independently captured. Dedicated sandbox-account installation does not establish which token applied the failed ACE.

## Requested supported guidance

1. Can a supported release/configuration enforce these denied-read paths with a non-admin sandbox payload, without taking ownership of OS-managed folders, weakening the declared denials or falling back to a weaker executor?
2. Is there a supported read-only diagnostic to establish the failing helper's runtime/impersonation identity without repeating the setup?
3. Can ACL application preflight or transactionally restore changes if a later target fails? If not, what supported recovery contract applies?

The official Windows sandbox page describes elevated provisioning, denied-read limitations of unelevated, and diagnostics, but the reviewed page did not resolve this exact failure. OpenAI's AI-assisted support messenger recommended this issue tracker and stated it could not create a human support case from that channel. That AI response is advisory; it is not engineering confirmation.

items.title: Retain rollout migration locks across worker cancellation
items.body:
Retain rollout migration locks across worker cancellation

## Why

Cancelling an async migration caller can leave its blocking compression or decompression worker running. Releasing migration locks before that worker finishes allows other writers or migrations to access files still being processed.

## What changed

Share maintenance, cross-process writer, and local writer locks with blocking workers during migration and recovery. Keep those locks held until file work completes, releasing cross-process locks before allowing local writers to proceed.

## Testing

Add a regression test for cancelled compression and decompression callers that verifies locks remain held until the worker finishes and the output is complete. Preserve the Unix check that decompression temporaries have owner-only permissions.

items.title: Fix cancellation of macOS user-verification prompts
items.body:
Fix cancellation of macOS user-verification prompts

## Why

Keychain signing reconstructs its own authentication context, so invalidating the caller's context does not reliably cancel the context that owns the biometric prompt.

## What changed

Evaluate the stored key's access-control policy explicitly with `LAContext` before signing. On cancellation, invalidate that context and wait for its authorization callback before releasing the lifecycle lock, rejecting any late success. Reload the key with the authorized context and disable further interaction so signing cannot open another prompt.

## Testing

Update unit tests to cover waiting for cancellation completion and rejecting completed authorization after cancellation. Add an ignored macOS hardware test and setup instructions covering persisted Secure Enclave key reuse, signature verification, cancellation, retry signing, and cleanup.

items.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

One of my existing conversations is stuck. Every recent attempt fails with:

```text
Error running remote compact task: stream disconnected before completion:
An error occurred while processing your request.
```

The interface also shows **Compaction interrupted** and **Reconnecting 2/2**. Restarting the Windows app did not recover the conversation. Even sending just "Hi" fails before the assistant replies.

I lost my open research tabs when I restarted. I need a way to recover and continue the existing work without losing the conversation history.

### Environment

- Product: Windows desktop app, local Codex conversation.
- Windows version reported by the runtime: Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26300.0; 64-bit.
- Local app-server version reported in the desktop startup log: `0.162.0-alpha.17.2`. This is the **app-server version**, not a verified desktop app version.
- Desktop app version and subscription: not independently verified.
- Observed: October 13, 2026, America/Phoenix (UTC-07:00).

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

This describes the observed failure in an existing conversation; I do not have a minimal fresh-conversation reproduction.

1. Open the affected existing conversation.
2. Submit a message.
3. Observe the remote compaction error and reconnect attempts.
4. Restart the desktop app and return to the same conversation.
5. Submit "Hi". It fails with the same remote compaction error.

### Confirmed diagnostic evidence

The six most recent inspected turns in that conversation have a terminal **failed** status and the same remote compaction error. Their completion times were:

| Time on October 13, 2026 (America/Phoenix) | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 1:39:34 PM | Remote compaction failed |
| 1:39:57 PM | Remote compaction failed |
| 1:40:19 PM | Remote compaction failed |
| 1:41:41 PM | Remote compaction failed; the message reported restarting and losing tabs |
| 2:13:55 PM | Remote compaction failed for a plain "Hi" |
| 2:16:06 PM | Remote compaction failed for "hi" with an attached screenshot |

Those failures took approximately 9 to 24 seconds. Six is the count in the inspected recent-turn sample, not a claimed total for all failures.

Two request IDs in the supplied screenshot exactly match the saved failed-turn records. The conversation history remains readable through the desktop thread-reading tool, but the affected conversation cannot generate a new response. Another conversation on the same installation is responding; this is not a controlled network or model comparison.

### What is the expected behavior?

The existing conversation should complete compaction and answer, or provide an actionable recovery option that preserves history and work. Restarting or submitting a short message should not leave the conversation permanently stuck at the same compaction step. Open research tabs should survive or be recoverable after a restart.

### Request

Please investigate the repeated compaction failure and provide a supported way to recover the existing conversation. If there is a known fix, please identify the affected component and fixed version.

The underlying cause has not been established. This report does not assume that the Windows client, connection, or service is solely responsible.

Request IDs, the affected conversation ID, and the screenshot are retained for a private support follow-up. This public report contains no raw conversation transcript.

Possibly related: #53653 and #52919. Similar symptoms do not establish a shared cause.
